notes.definition: Plants defend themselves against pathogens and animals using physical defences (cellulose cell walls, a waxy cuticle and bark), chemical defences (antibacterial chemicals and poisons) and mechanical adaptations (thorns, hairs, leaves that droop or curl when touched, and mimicry).
explanation: Plants cannot move away from pathogens or from animals that want to eat them, so they have evolved defences. These are grouped into three types: physical defences, chemical defences and mechanical adaptations. Physical and chemical defences mainly stop pathogens from getting in or surviving, while mechanical adaptations mainly deter animals such as herbivores.

Physical defence responses act as barriers to pathogens. Every plant cell has a cellulose cell wall, which is strong and hard for many microorganisms to get through. Leaves are covered by a tough waxy cuticle, which forms a barrier that pathogens cannot easily cross and stops water collecting on the leaf surface where microorganisms could grow. Stems are covered by layers of dead cells, for example bark on trees. These dead cells form a protective layer that is hard to penetrate, and they fall off, taking any pathogens on them with them.

Chemical plant defence responses include antibacterial chemicals and poisons. Some plants produce antibacterial chemicals that kill bacteria or stop them growing; for example mint and witch hazel produce antibacterial chemicals. Other plants produce poisons that deter herbivores from eating them; for example tobacco plants, foxgloves and deadly nightshade contain poisons, so animals learn to avoid them.

Mechanical adaptations protect plants from animals. Thorns (as on roses and blackberries) and hairs on stems and leaves deter animals from touching or eating the plant. Some leaves droop or curl when touched: the sensitive plant Mimosa pudica folds its leaves quickly, which can dislodge insects and startle or deter animals that would eat it. Mimicry tricks animals: some plants look like something else, for example the white dead-nettle looks like a stinging nettle so animals avoid it, and some passion flowers have yellow spots that look like butterfly eggs, so butterflies do not lay their eggs there.

These defences are adaptations that increase a plant's chance of survival and reproduction. The barriers are always present and are the plant's first line of defence against pathogens getting in, while the chemicals and mechanical adaptations reduce damage from pathogens and herbivores. Damage to these defences, for example a broken cuticle or wounds in bark, gives pathogens a way to enter the plant.
keyFacts: Physical defences: cellulose cell walls, tough waxy cuticle on leaves, layers of dead cells on stems (bark) which fall off.
Physical defences act as barriers to stop pathogens entering plant cells and tissues.
Dead cells on the surface of stems fall off, removing pathogens with them.
Chemical defences: antibacterial chemicals and poisons to deter herbivores.
Mint and witch hazel produce antibacterial chemicals.
Tobacco, foxgloves and deadly nightshade produce poisons that deter herbivores.
Mechanical adaptations: thorns and hairs deter animals.
Some leaves droop or curl when touched, for example Mimosa pudica.
Mimicry tricks animals, for example white dead-nettle looks like a stinging nettle.

keyTerms.definition: A structural barrier that stops pathogens entering a plant, such as a cellulose cell wall, waxy cuticle or bark.
A substance made by a plant to protect it, such as an antibacterial chemical or a poison that deters herbivores.
A feature that protects a plant from animals, such as thorns, hairs, leaves that droop or curl when touched, or mimicry.
A tough, waterproof waxy layer on the surface of leaves that acts as a barrier to pathogens.
Layers of dead cells on the surface of tree stems that protect against pathogens and fall off.
When an organism looks like another organism or object, tricking animals into avoiding it.
A chemical that kills bacteria or stops them growing.

workedExamples.title: Classifying defences
workedExamples.question: Classify each defence as physical, chemical or mechanical: (a) holly leaves with sharp spikes; (b) bark on an oak tree; (c) foxgloves containing a poison; (d) a waxy cuticle on leaves.
steps: Ask: is it a barrier to pathogens? Then it is physical (bark, cuticle, cell walls).
Ask: is it a substance the plant makes? Then it is chemical (antibacterial chemicals, poisons).
Ask: does it deter or trick animals by its structure or movement? Then it is a mechanical adaptation (thorns, hairs, drooping leaves, mimicry).
(a) spikes are like thorns: mechanical. (b) bark: physical. (c) poison: chemical. (d) waxy cuticle: physical.

workedExamples.title: Explaining how bark protects a tree
workedExamples.question: Explain how bark helps to protect a tree from pathogens.
steps: Bark is made of layers of dead cells on the surface of the stem.
It forms a tough barrier that pathogens find hard to get through.
The dead cells fall off, so any pathogens on the surface are removed with them.
workedExamples.answer: Bark is a barrier of dead cells that pathogens cannot easily penetrate, and as the dead cells fall off, pathogens on them are lost too.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think plants have an immune system with white blood cells like humans.
misconceptions.right: In fact plants rely on physical barriers, chemicals and mechanical adaptations. They do not have white blood cells or antibodies.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often classify thorns as a physical defence against pathogens.
misconceptions.right: In fact AQA classifies thorns and hairs as mechanical adaptations that deter animals. Physical defences are cellulose cell walls, the waxy cuticle and bark.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think bark is made of living cells.
misconceptions.right: In fact bark is made of layers of dead cells, which fall off and take pathogens with them.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all plant chemicals are poisons for animals.
misconceptions.right: In fact some are antibacterial chemicals that act against bacteria, while poisons are aimed at deterring herbivores.

realWorld: Witch hazel extract is used in skin products because of its antibacterial and soothing chemicals.
Many medicines and pesticides are based on plant defence chemicals; nicotine from tobacco plants was once used as an insecticide.
Gardeners plant thorny hedges such as hawthorn and holly to deter animals and people.
Tree surgeons seal or carefully prune cuts in bark because wounds let pathogens into the tree.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Biology only (not Combined Science Trilogy): physical and chemical plant defence responses and mechanical adaptations.
examTips: Learn the three categories and their exact examples: physical (cell walls, waxy cuticle, bark), chemical (antibacterial chemicals, poisons), mechanical (thorns, hairs, drooping/curling leaves, mimicry).
When explaining physical defences, use the word 'barrier' and say what it stops (pathogens entering).
For bark, mention both that it is a barrier of dead cells AND that the cells fall off, removing pathogens.
For mimicry, say what is copied and what the animal is tricked into doing (or not doing).
Read whether the question asks about defence against pathogens or against animals, and choose examples to match.
summary: Plants defend themselves with physical, chemical and mechanical defences.
Physical: cellulose cell walls, waxy cuticle and bark form barriers to pathogens.
Bark is dead cells that fall off, removing pathogens.
Chemical: antibacterial chemicals kill bacteria; poisons deter herbivores.
Mechanical: thorns and hairs deter animals; some leaves droop or curl when touched.
Mimicry tricks animals into avoiding the plant.

questions.question: Which of these is a physical defence of plants?
markScheme: 1 mark: Waxy cuticle
questions.explanation: The waxy cuticle is a physical barrier. Leaves that droop when touched and mimicry are mechanical adaptations, and poisons are chemical defences. (Thorns are also classed by AQA as a mechanical adaptation, not a physical defence.)

questions.question: What are plant cell walls made of?
markScheme: 1 mark: Cellulose
questions.explanation: Plant cell walls are made of cellulose, which forms a barrier to pathogens. Chitin is found in fungal cell walls.

questions.question: Which of these is a chemical defence of plants?
markScheme: 1 mark: Antibacterial chemicals
questions.explanation: Antibacterial chemicals are chemical defences. Bark is physical, and hairs and curling leaves are mechanical adaptations.

questions.question: What is bark made of?
markScheme: 1 mark: Layers of dead cells
questions.explanation: Bark is layers of dead cells on the surface of stems. They fall off, removing pathogens.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of poisons made by plants such as foxgloves and deadly nightshade?
markScheme: 1 mark: To deter herbivores
questions.explanation: Poisons deter animals from eating the plant. Antibacterial chemicals are the defence against bacteria.

questions.question: The white dead-nettle does not sting but looks very similar to the stinging nettle. What type of defence is this?
markScheme: 1 mark: Mimicry
questions.explanation: The plant copies the appearance of a stinging nettle, tricking animals into avoiding it. Mimicry is a mechanical adaptation.

questions.question: Which pair of plants are both known for producing antibacterial chemicals?
markScheme: 1 mark: Mint and witch hazel
questions.explanation: Mint and witch hazel produce antibacterial chemicals. Foxglove and tobacco produce poisons; roses and holly have thorns or spikes; Mimosa and passion flower show mechanical adaptations.

It may dislodge insects and deter animals from eating it
It releases a poison into the soil
markScheme: 1 mark: It may dislodge insects and deter animals from eating it
questions.explanation: Drooping or curling when touched is a mechanical adaptation that can shake off insects and startle or deter herbivores.

questions.question: A gardener damages the bark of a tree with a lawnmower. Soon afterwards the tree becomes infected by a fungus. What is the best explanation?
options: The lawnmower carried poison into the tree
The damage removed the tree's antibacterial chemicals
The fungus was attracted by the smell of the cut
The barrier of dead cells was broken, so the pathogen could enter
markScheme: 1 mark: The barrier of dead cells was broken, so the pathogen could enter
questions.explanation: Bark is a physical barrier. A wound exposes living tissue, giving pathogens a way in. Antibacterial chemicals would not act against a fungus anyway.

The spots look like butterfly eggs, so butterflies 'think' the leaf is already used
The spots are thorns that injure butterflies

questions.question: Name three physical defence responses of plants.
markScheme: 1 mark: cellulose cell walls
1 mark: tough waxy cuticle on leaves
1 mark: layers of dead cells on stems / bark
questions.explanation: These three structures act as barriers that stop pathogens entering.

questions.question: Name two types of chemical defence produced by plants.
markScheme: 1 mark: antibacterial chemicals
1 mark: poisons (to deter herbivores)
questions.explanation: Antibacterial chemicals act against bacteria, and poisons deter herbivores.

questions.question: Give two mechanical adaptations that plants use to deter animals.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two from: thorns; hairs; leaves which droop or curl when touched; mimicry
questions.explanation: Mechanical adaptations protect against animals rather than pathogens.

questions.question: Name a plant that produces a poison to deter herbivores.
markScheme: 1 mark: foxglove / tobacco / deadly nightshade
questions.explanation: These plants contain poisons, so animals that eat them become ill and learn to avoid them.

questions.question: Explain how the layers of dead cells on the surface of a stem protect the plant from pathogens.
markScheme: 1 mark: they form a barrier that pathogens cannot easily get through
1 mark: the dead cells fall off, taking pathogens with them
questions.explanation: Both points are in the specification: barrier, and dead cells falling off.

questions.question: Explain how a waxy cuticle helps to protect a leaf from pathogens.
markScheme: 1 mark: it is a tough barrier covering the leaf
1 mark: so pathogens cannot easily enter the leaf cells (and water does not collect for pathogens to grow in)
questions.explanation: The cuticle is a physical barrier over the epidermis.

questions.question:
Roses have thorns.
A scientist removed the thorns from some rose plants. She left the thorns on other rose plants.
Table 1 shows the number of plants that were damaged by deer after three months.
Explain how thorns help the rose plant to survive.

headers: Number of plants damaged by deer

markScheme: 1 mark: thorns deter animals/herbivores from eating the plant
1 mark: so less of the plant is eaten / more leaves remain for photosynthesis and growth
questions.explanation: Thorns are a mechanical adaptation; being eaten less increases survival and reproduction.

questions.question:
A student grew bacteria on agar plates. She added mint extract to some plates and water to the other plates.
Table 1 shows the results.
Suggest why a plant that produces antibacterial chemicals is less likely to be killed by bacterial diseases.
markScheme: 1 mark: the chemicals kill bacteria / stop bacteria growing, so infections do not develop
questions.explanation: Antibacterial chemicals prevent bacterial pathogens from multiplying in the plant.

questions.question:
A scientist compared the number of insect eggs laid on two varieties of the same plant.
One variety has hairs on its leaves. The other variety has no hairs.
Table 1 shows the results.
Suggest how hairs on leaves deter insects.

headers: Mean number of insect eggs per leaf

markScheme: 1 mark: hairs make it difficult for insects to move over / reach the surface of the leaf
1 mark: so it is harder for them to feed or lay eggs
questions.explanation: A hairy surface is a mechanical barrier to small animals.

questions.question: Aphids feed by pushing their mouthparts into plant stems and leaves. Suggest why some aphids can still feed on plants that have a waxy cuticle and cellulose cell walls.
markScheme: 1 mark: aphids have mouthparts that can pierce/penetrate the cuticle and cell walls
1 mark: so they reach the phloem sap; physical barriers mainly stop microorganisms, not insects
questions.explanation: Physical defences are barriers to pathogens. Insects with piercing mouthparts can get through them, which is also how aphids spread viruses into plants.

questions.question: A student says, 'Plant defences only protect against pathogens.' Use examples to explain why the student is wrong.
markScheme: 1 mark: some defences protect against animals/herbivores
1 mark: chemical example, e.g. poisons in foxgloves/tobacco deter herbivores
1 mark: mechanical example, e.g. thorns, hairs, drooping leaves or mimicry deter or trick animals
questions.explanation: Physical barriers and antibacterial chemicals act against pathogens, but poisons and mechanical adaptations target animals.

questions.question: Suggest why animals that eat a poisonous plant once may avoid that type of plant in future, and how this benefits the plant species.
markScheme: 1 mark: the animal becomes ill and learns to associate the plant with being ill
1 mark: so fewer of these plants are eaten, and more survive to reproduce
questions.explanation: Poisons deter herbivores; the species benefits as more plants survive.

questions.question: What type of animal do plant poisons mainly deter?
markScheme: 1 mark: herbivores (plant-eating animals)

questions.question: Describe the physical and chemical defence responses of plants.
markScheme: Indicative content: physical: cellulose cell walls form a barrier; tough waxy cuticle on leaves is a barrier to pathogens; layers of dead cells on stems (bark) form a barrier and fall off, removing pathogens; chemical: antibacterial chemicals kill bacteria (e.g. mint, witch hazel); poisons deter herbivores (e.g. tobacco, foxglove, deadly nightshade).
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): both physical and chemical defences described, with how they work.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some defences named, little description, or only one type covered.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The question asks for both physical and chemical, so cover both with an explanation of how each protects the plant.

questions.question: Plants cannot move away from pathogens or animals. Describe and explain the different ways in which plants defend themselves, using examples.
markScheme: Indicative content: physical defences: cellulose cell walls; tough waxy cuticle on leaves; layers of dead cells on stems (bark) which fall off; these are barriers that stop pathogens entering; bark falling off removes pathogens. Chemical defences: antibacterial chemicals (mint, witch hazel) kill bacteria; poisons (tobacco, foxglove, deadly nightshade) deter herbivores. Mechanical adaptations: thorns (roses) and hairs deter animals; leaves which droop or curl when touched (Mimosa) dislodge insects/deter herbivores; mimicry tricks animals, e.g. white dead-nettle resembles stinging nettle, passion flower spots resemble butterfly eggs. Overall: protects against infection and being eaten, increasing survival.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): all three types described with examples and clear explanations of how each protects the plant.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): at least two types described with some explanation and examples.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some defences listed with little explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Organise the answer by the three categories and, for each defence, say what it protects against and how.

questions.question: Describe the mechanical adaptations that plants have to protect themselves from animals.
markScheme: Indicative content: thorns (e.g. roses, blackberries) deter animals from touching/eating; hairs on stems and leaves deter animals/insects; leaves which droop or curl when touched (e.g. Mimosa pudica) can dislodge insects or startle herbivores; mimicry tricks animals, e.g. white dead-nettle looks like stinging nettle so is avoided, passion flower spots look like butterfly eggs so butterflies do not lay eggs.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): at least three adaptations described with how they protect the plant.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): adaptations named with little description.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Include all four types of mechanical adaptation listed by AQA and explain the effect on the animal.
